content: The recommendations provided are specifically applicable to the use of second-line line probe assays (SL-LPA) in children diagnosed with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). These recommendations are based on the extrapolation of data obtained from studies conducted in adults. Mutations detected by SL-LPA that confer resistance are strongly correlated with phenotypic resistance to fluoroquinolones, such as ofloxacin and levofloxacin. Similarly, these resistance-conferring mutations are also highly correlated with phenotypic resistance to second-line injectable drugs (SLIDs). Due to the high specificity of SL-LPA in detecting resistance to fluoroquinolones and SLIDs, positive results from this assay can be used to guide the implementation of appropriate infection control measures. The SL-LPA test operates on the same principles as the first-line line probe assay (LPA). The procedure can be performed directly on processed sputum samples or indirectly using DNA isolated and amplified from Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures. The steps include: 1. Decontamination and concentration of sputum specimens (e.g., using sodium hydroxide and centrifugation). 2. Isolation and amplification of DNA. 3. Detection of amplified products via reverse hybridization. 4. Visualization using a streptavidin-conjugated alkaline phosphatase color reaction. For indirect testing, only steps 2–4 are required. The observed banding patterns, corresponding to wild-type or resistance-genotype probes, are used to determine the drug susceptibility profile of the analyzed specimen. The entire assay can be completed within a single working day. SL-LPAs are designed to detect specific mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolones (e.g., ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin) and SLIDs (e.g., kanamycin, amikacin, and capreomycin) in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC). These assays identify mutations in the gyrA quinolone resistance-determining region (codons 85–97), the rrs gene (codons 1401, 1402, and 1484), and additional regions such as gyrB (codons 536–541) and the eis promoter region (codons –10 to –14). The eis C14T mutation, for example, is associated with kanamycin resistance in strains from Eastern Europe. SL-LPAs can also detect mutations in the embB gene, which may encode resistance to ethambutol. However, the accuracy of SL-LPAs for detecting ethambutol resistance has not been fully established. The test is effective for both smear-positive and smear-negative specimens, as well as culture isolates. It provides rapid results, typically within five hours, compared to several weeks with conventional methods. This rapid turnaround time is particularly beneficial for the early detection of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) in patients previously diagnosed with MDR-TB. The GenoType MTBDRsl assay, a specific type of SL-LPA, is based on PCR and DNA-STRIP technology. Mycobacterial DNA is extracted from patient specimens or cultured material, amplified via PCR, and detected on a membrane strip using reverse hybridization and an enzymatic color reaction. Internal controls ensure the validity of results, and automated systems like GenoScan® can be used to interpret banding patterns, reducing transcription errors. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reviewed the accuracy and clinical utility of SL-LPAs for detecting mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolones and SLIDs in MDR/RR-TB patients. Positive SL-LPA results for fluoroquinolone or SLID resistance can be confidently used to guide treatment decisions. However, in cases of negative results, phenotypic culture-based drug susceptibility testing (DST) may still be necessary, especially in settings with a high pretest probability of resistance. The use of SL-LPAs in routine care can significantly reduce the time to diagnosis of fluoroquinolone and SLID resistance, particularly when used for direct testing of sputum specimens. Early detection of drug resistance allows for the timely initiation of appropriate therapy, improving patient outcomes. However, the indeterminate rate is higher when testing smear-negative specimens compared to smear-positive ones, necessitating repeat or additional testing in some cases. Overall, SL-LPAs are a valuable tool for the rapid and accurate detection of drug resistance in tuberculosis, particularly in patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB.
